accroche: We say “Epicurean” for a bon vivant. Epicurus himself mostly praised bread and water.
contenu_vulgarise:
A twelve-course meal, a cellar toured before the aperitif, a chef coming out to describe how the lobster was cooked: in everyday language, that is what being “Epicurean” means. The word has become a synonym for a lavish table and unrestrained pleasures.

Epicurus, for his part, writes in his *Letter to Menoeceus*, transmitted by Diogenes Laertius in Book X of his *Lives of the Eminent Philosophers*: “bread and water provide the greatest pleasure when brought to hungry lips.” Not lobster. Bread and water.

## The Mechanism

For Epicurus, pleasure is not a sensation to be maximized; it is a lack to be made to disappear. His definition is explicit: “by pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.” Once hunger and thirst are calmed, pleasure is complete; multiplying dishes does not increase it, it only varies it.

This definition governs his entire ethics. The letter sorts desires into three groups. Natural and necessary desires, eating, drinking, having shelter, are enough for happiness and are satisfied without difficulty, because nature has provided few things for them. Natural but unnecessary desires, a refined dish rather than a simple one, may be satisfied on occasion, without urgency. Finally, desires that are neither natural nor necessary concern objects that nothing limits, unlimited wealth, perpetual glory: they know no end, since no quantity ever satisfies them.

That is why Epicurus recommends frugality, not out of asceticism but out of calculation. Whoever gets used to little has nothing to fear from scarcity, and enjoys to the full the day abundance shows up, without becoming its slave the day it runs short.

## What This Shifts

The misreading is old. Seneca, Epictetus, and the first Christian authors already called the Epicureans voluptuous pigs, and the adjective has kept that sense down to us. Yet it misses the point of the argument. Epicurus does not say that pleasure is bad; he says that most of what we call pleasure, the feast, luxury, prestige, adds more anxiety than it removes, since one then fears losing what one has just acquired.

Frugality is therefore not a renunciation; it is the condition for truly attaining pleasure, since complete pleasure is defined by the absence of lack, not by filling it. A man content with bread and water is no less a hedonist than a gastronome; he has merely understood, according to Epicurus, that the other condemns himself to wanting ever more in order to feel, at bottom, the same thing.

carte.punch: An “Epicurean,” for Epicurus himself, made do with bread and water.
carte.idee: We call “Epicurean” a bon vivant given to the pleasures of the table. Yet Epicurus, in his Letter to Menoeceus, defines pleasure as the absence of pain, and praises bread and water taken by hungry lips above any feast.

quiz.question: Why does Epicurus recommend a frugal life rather than luxury?
choix: Because seeking pleasure would be immoral according to his doctrine
Because complete pleasure is the absence of lack, which luxury only varies
Because he had made a personal vow of poverty, like a monk
Because wealth remained reserved for free-born citizens alone
quiz.explication: Epicurus defines pleasure as the absence of pain: once the lack is removed, it is already complete. Luxury does not increase it, it varies it, and further exposes one to the fear of losing what one has just acquired. Nothing in his thought condemns pleasure or imposes a vow of poverty.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the Letter to Menoeceus, which group of desires does Epicurus say is the easiest to satisfy?
choix: Natural but unnecessary desires, such as a refined dish
Natural and necessary desires, such as eating, drinking, and having shelter
Desires that are neither natural nor necessary, such as unlimited wealth
All desires are satisfied with equal ease, according to Epicurus
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Nature has provided few things for natural and necessary desires, eating, drinking, having shelter, which makes them easy to satisfy. The other two groups demand more, or know no end.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Through which author has Epicurus's Letter to Menoeceus come down to us?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The letter is transmitted by Diogenes Laertius in Book X of his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. Seneca and Epictetus, according to the entry, merely called the Epicureans voluptuous pigs.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Seneca, Epictetus, and the first Christian authors already describe the Epicureans, according to the entry?
choix: As philosophers dangerous to the state
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry reports that these authors called the Epicureans voluptuous pigs, a misreading that misses the point of the argument and that the adjective has kept down to us.
